We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-1894)
response:
The central question is: when you prune a transformer after training (rather than during), which attention heads can you remove without destabilizing the remaining layers, and does the answer change depending on how deep into training you are when you start cutting? The key concepts are head redundancy (multiple heads in the same layer computing near-identical attention patterns or output projections, measurable via cosine similarity of their value-weighted outputs), layer-wise pruning stability (whether the loss surface around a pruned checkpoint is smooth enough that the surviving heads can absorb the removed heads' function without cascading degradation across layers), and post-training compression (pruning applied after the model is fully trained, as opposed to structured sparsity imposed during the forward pass during training). The beginner assumes redundancy is a static property — that heads which look redundant by some similarity metric are safely removable — but the expert worries about functional redundancy versus statistical redundancy: two heads may produce correlated outputs on the calibration distribution while serving as backup for each other under distribution shift, so pruning both collapses robustness even if held-out perplexity barely moves. The deeper expert concern is layer coupling: pruning heads in layer k changes the residual stream statistics that layer k+1 was trained to expect, and this mismatch compounds — early layers are particularly dangerous because their errors propagate through every subsequent layer's layernorm rescaling. Stability under pruning is therefore not just about which heads are redundant but about the order in which you prune and whether you interleave lightweight fine-tuning to re-center the residual stream before cutting the next layer.

The primary determinant is whether the fine-tuning signal comes from a distribution with sufficient task diversity and tail coverage relative to the model's intended deployment — calibration sets that are narrow (e.g., a single domain like C4 or a few thousand Wikipedia sentences, common in LLM.int8() and GPTQ setups) will allow the surviving heads to re-specialize toward that narrow distribution, moving weight mass in directions that hurt rare constructions without any training signal pushing back. A concrete diagnostic is tracking the rank of the gradient updates during the interleaved fine-tuning: legitimate stabilization produces low-rank updates concentrated in the LayerNorm parameters and the unaffected heads' output projections, while overfitting to calibration produces higher-rank, more dispersed updates that touch query/key projections — the latter is the model rewriting attention patterns rather than re-centering scale. LLM-Pruner (Ma et al., 2023) reported exactly this failure mode: their post-pruning LoRA recovery steps on a 7B LLaMA model showed strong benchmark recovery on commonsense reasoning but silent degradation on code generation, which wasn't in their recovery corpus, with perplexity on The Stack increasing ~18% even as MMLU scores recovered to within 2% of baseline. The sharpest early-warning signal is held-out gradient alignment: compute the cosine similarity between the fine-tuning gradient and the gradient computed on a small, diverse held-out probe set (covering domains absent from calibration) — if this alignment drops below ~0.3 over successive fine-tuning steps, the updates are moving in directions orthogonal or opposed to generalization. A subtler structural check is whether LayerNorm gain parameters (γ) across the pruned layers are converging back toward their pre-pruning values or drifting further: genuine residual stream re-centering should pull γ back toward ~1.0 in the affected layers, whereas calibration overfitting lets γ drift to compensate for distribution shift the model has learned to expect rather than actually correcting the underlying mismatch.

The most principled structural intervention is singular value rescaling of the surviving heads' W_Q, W_K, and W_V matrices immediately after pruning: you compute the SVD of each matrix, identify singular values that have inflated relative to the pre-pruning distribution (which happens because the head is now carrying load it wasn't trained to carry), and shrink them back toward the median singular value of that weight matrix class across the unpruned model — this directly limits the capacity of any single direction to dominate, reducing the surface area available for overfitting. A second concrete intervention is weight interpolation toward the pre-pruning checkpoint, specifically for the surviving heads: SliceGPT (Ashkboos et al., 2024) implicitly exploits this by working in the PCA-reduced residual stream basis, and their approach can be read as enforcing that surviving weight directions stay close to the original weight manifold before any fine-tuning occurs, which constrains subsequent gradient updates to corrections rather than rewrites. A third option is explicit null-space projection: after pruning head h, compute the subspace of W_O that the pruned head occupied, then project the surviving heads' W_O matrices to remove components that lie in that subspace — this prevents the surviving heads from immediately collapsing into the vacated directions (which is the first move overfitting makes), forcing fine-tuning to find genuinely new directions if it needs to recover that function. Quantitatively, Sun et al. (2024) in Wanda showed that weight rescaling interventions applied before any gradient step reduced the perplexity gap between pruned and fine-tuned models by roughly 30-40% on WikiText-2 at 50% sparsity, suggesting the pre-gradient structural step does substantial work that fine-tuning would otherwise have to do, and do less cleanly. The key principle unifying all three is constraining the effective degrees of freedom available to fine-tuning so that the narrow calibration set isn't asked to determine directions in a high-dimensional space it can't adequately sample — you want fine-tuning to tune scalars and low-rank corrections, not rewrite the entire attention geometry.

The most principled alternative baseline is the ensemble of singular value spectra across all layers at the same depth class in the current (partially pruned) model — rather than comparing a layer to its own past, you compare it to the distribution of singular values across all attention layers at similar depth, exploiting the empirical regularity (documented in Timor et al., 2023 on BERT-family models) that weight matrix spectra are remarkably consistent within depth bands in healthy transformers, with coefficient of variation below 0.15 for the top-k singular values within a layer class. A second candidate is the activation covariance of the residual stream computed on calibration data after each pruning step: instead of referencing weight-space baselines, you ask whether the empirical covariance of hidden states at layer k matches the covariance at that same layer in the original model (stored cheaply as its top-50 principal components), and use divergence from that as your "inflation" signal — this is distribution-referenced rather than weight-referenced, sidestepping the drifting-checkpoint problem entirely. The failure mode of the cross-layer spectral reference is systematic co-drift: if several layers are pruned sequentially, their spectra all drift together, so the within-depth-band distribution shifts as a unit and the outlier detection loses sensitivity — you'd declare the inflated layer normal because all its peers are equally inflated, which is precisely the compounding error you were trying to catch. The activation covariance approach fails when the calibration set is too narrow to accurately estimate the residual stream covariance at later layers, because later-layer representations are more input-specific and higher-variance; with fewer than roughly 2048 diverse tokens per covariance estimate (a threshold suggested by experiments in the LASER paper, Sharma et al., 2023), the top principal components are unreliable and the divergence signal becomes noisy enough to either miss real drift or flag healthy layers. A hybrid that partially addresses both failure modes is using layer-wise optimal transport distance between the current weight singular value distribution and that of a frozen "anchor" model (e.g., a smaller but fully intact model from the same family, such as using Llama-7B spectra as anchor when pruning Llama-13B), exploiting the cross-scale spectral similarity documented in scaling law analyses — but this fails if the anchor and target model diverged significantly during instruction tuning or RLHF, where certain layers develop idiosyncratic spectra absent in the smaller model.
